reading.title: Big Ideas Packed Into Three Letters
reading.purpose: Discover how the suffix -ism turns root words into beliefs, movements, and habits of mind.
paras: Three simple letters at the end of a word—the suffix -ism—often signal a whole system of thought, a political force, or a steady habit of mind. In history classes, students meet several powerful -ism words side by side. Nationalism describes intense pride in and loyalty to one's own nation, sometimes placing it above every neighbor. Imperialism names a policy in which one country extends its power by taking control of distant lands and peoples. Despotism refers to unchecked rule by a single leader who holds complete power without limits or fairness.

Not every political belief calls for force. Pacifism is the conviction that war and violence are always wrong and that nations must settle disputes peacefully. Outside politics, other -ism words describe how people look at daily life. Someone guided by optimism expects good results and spots openings even in tough moments, whereas pessimism leans the opposite way, expecting the worst before trying. Between those two sits realism, the habit of facing situations exactly as they are without painting them brighter or darker.

The suffix also names habits and professions we encounter every week. Materialism is the tendency to prize money and possessions above friendships, learning, or purpose. Meanwhile, honest journalism—the public work of gathering, checking, and reporting news—depends on verifying facts and crediting every source.

That last rule matters in school as much as in a newsroom. Plagiarism, copying another writer's words or ideas and claiming them as your own, breaks trust wherever it appears. Learning to unpack the suffix -ism gives readers a quick key for recognizing how ideas, attitudes, and practices shape the world.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "realism" most nearly means
choices: expecting the worst outcome before even starting a project
facing situations as they truly are without exaggerating them
valuing expensive objects more than friendships or learning
refusing to use force or violence to settle any disagreement
qs.why: Paragraph 2 defines realism directly as "the habit of facing situations exactly as they are without painting them brighter or darker."

qs.q: Which sentence defines a system in which one ruler holds unlimited power?
choices: Three simple letters at the end of a word—the suffix -ism—often signal a whole system of thought, a political force, or a steady habit of mind.
Nationalism describes intense pride in and loyalty to one's own nation, sometimes placing it above every neighbor.
Imperialism names a policy in which one country extends its power by taking control of distant lands and peoples.
Despotism refers to unchecked rule by a single leader who holds complete power without limits or fairness.
qs.why: This sentence defines despotism as unchecked rule by a single leader holding complete power without limits.

ev.text: Despotism refers to unchecked rule by a single leader who holds complete power without limits or fairness.

qs.q: Why does the author connect journalism and schoolwork in the final two paragraphs?
choices: Both depend on honesty and crediting sources instead of copying someone else's work.
Both require students to travel to distant lands to report on political movements.
Both encourage writers to adopt pessimism whenever they read a history textbook.
Both prove that three-letter suffixes are only used in modern newspaper offices.
qs.why: Paragraph 3 notes that honest journalism credits every source, and paragraph 4 explains that plagiarism breaks trust in school just as in a newsroom.

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Political beliefs are much harder to understand than everyday habits like optimism.
The suffix -ism marks a wide range of beliefs, systems, attitudes, and practices.
Every word ending in -ism describes a harmful habit that societies should avoid.
Newsrooms should stop using long historical words when reporting on daily events.
qs.why: The reading groups political systems, outlooks, values, and professions to show how the suffix -ism signals systems of thought or practice.
